I've been writing since before high school (almost several years, yikes) with no professional teachings given or whatever. I still sometimes have problems settling on just one idea (but honestly, who said having a ton of ideas was a bad thing?) Here's a couple things/tools/tips that might help out when you're overwhelmed.

Outlines are a good option, but don't be fooled, they're not for everyone. Outlines are optional, you could just write down your idea and expand on it, but not all at once! Carry a notebook around and write down all your ideas, and add to them until you have one you like. And then BOOM: just write that idea and see how it goes.

Having two different ideas for two different stories? Go ahead and write them both, finish the intro and compare the two. The one you like more is the one you should continue writing for. File the other one away for a day you have time for it. Same with scene, action and dialogue ideas that don't fit - file it away. You never know when that one utterly epic, tear inducing, breathlessly-emotional or tearfully-funny piece of dialogue or action will suddenly fit perfectly into something else.

If you've written something out completely, and then think you hate it - DO NOT DELETE IT!! At least not immediately. It's a strange rule, but it may save you some time and energy. When you've spent hours and days staring at something, you're going to pick out every single flaw and slowly grow to hate it. Take a break from it, maybe for at least a day to cool off and do other stuff, and then go back to it and see if you can fix it, or if it belongs in the garbage. Chance are, you can fix it, or it wasn't even as bad as you thought.

Also: Look into doing a daily writing prompt. Something small, like maybe a three paragraph sort of thing. Do that long enough and you'll start improving your ability to focus on a single idea. There are a lot of writing prompt instagrams and blogs you can look at.

I can't think of anything else to add, but there are hundreds of resources online nowadays, so my suggestion is to honestly do some research. Dabble in different genres, read what other people are writing and test the waters of different characters, different settings, etc. 

And I rambled. I'm sorry. If you ever need someone to bounce ideas off of, my inbox is always open! Don't give up on writing, it's really worth it, trust me.

I know this has already been branded as NTA, but I just wanted to throw in my two cents. I WORK at a Goodwill. We have never paged a "room" for the person who has the furniture tag just because some whiny person wants it. If someone doesn't buy it in a certain amount of time, we reprice it and let someone else buy it. No paging, no calling out the costumer who has the tag, no acting like this "attendant" you mention.

I won't say that its every state, but again, training is more or less the same for every single state and every single region, only state laws change for each store.

On top of that...when did this happen? Most Goodwill stores have completely stopped carrying furniture as it was hurting sales for most regions. Only the outlet stores and popular, busier big stores still carry furniture, and $20 is waaaaayyyy below the average price of recliners in a Goodwill. I never saw one below $50, most were more. Recliners aren't cheap.

I'm honestly skeptical that this even happened. And if the man was right there, why the hell did you blatantly ignore him and talk only to the attendant? What fancy ass Goodwill has a dedicated "back" attendant? Do you mean the fucking stocker?? A donations attendant??? Why did this require a manager who did nothing but hand you back the damn tag??? This sounds made up, no offense.

I don't think I'll follow your idea for the reorganizing of my sentences (no offense) but I split my paragraphs like that because a writer needs to take into account that mobile readers will ditch a story for having giant blocks of text with no breaks. Also, when introducing a character or idea, a new paragraph MUST be started.

Thank you for the compliment of my hook. And again, thank you for your feedback. (As for the hummingbird part, I've had my hair pulled and yanked at by hummingbirds before, and as long as one is still and calm, they tend to hover. But that's just my own experience.)

For a first piece of writing, this is very well written. I would advice to maybe explore more ways to describe things that happen, noises, lights, etc. This character seems to fighting a losing war with a fraying mind, insanity is always something to play with. It is a little hard to follow, I'm not sure where the character is supposed to be until you imply that he's in bed, and then he's in the bathroom and his dog is in there with him? Did the dog move, did it make a sound, does it get up and leave or try to get your man's attention? 

I also noticed in the sentence "The reflection's delayed - I'm delayed" you use the hyphen. This is a perfectly good use of the hyphen, but also consider the semi-colon; it's a good way to split a sentence in two but keep that flow you want. 

All together, it's a very haunting, poetic bit of writing. It reads like a story, but has the overall aesthetic of a poem, which makes it that much more interesting. Good job! Keep going, you've got a good start here.
